articles.title: Israeli settlers establish outpost in Palestinian-controlled Area A of West Bank
articles.summary:
Israeli settlers establish outpost in Palestinian-controlled Area A of West Bank

Submitted by Nadav Rapaport on Wed, 11/18/2026 - 14:18
The Israeli military has yet to remove the outpost, despite acknowledging that its presence in Area A is illegal
Israeli settlers watch Palestinian farmers picking olives in the village of Turmus Ayya, northeast of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, on 21 October 2026 (Zain Jaafar/AFP)
Off

Israeli settlers have established an outpost in a Palestinian-administered area of the occupied West Bank, with the military yet to remove them, Haaretz reported on Wednesday.

According to the report, settlers established a branch of the Homesh yeshiva near the Palestinian village of Yasid, northwest of Nablus, seizing land belonging to the village in Area A.

Under the 1990s Oslo Accords, the occupied West Bank was divided into three areas: Area A, under Palestinian civil and security control; Area B, under Palestinian civil and Israeli security control; and Area C, under full Israeli control.

The Israeli military told Haaretz that it had previously evacuated the outpost, but settlers had since re-established it.

"Entry into Area A is prohibited by law, dangerous to civilians and constitutes a criminal offence," an Israeli army spokesperson said. 

"The outpost was evacuated once," the spokesperson said, adding that enforcement efforts against illegal settlements in the West Bank "continue at all times".

However, the military did not say whether it intended to remove the outpost again.

Ras Abu Nimel, a Palestinian landowner in the area, told Haaretz that settlers had seized land designated for a new residential neighbourhood, halting the project.

"Everything was ready for the start of marketing the plots, but the settlers’ takeover halted the project," Abu Nimel said. He estimated that settlers had seized around 15 dunams of land belonging to several villages.

"Even before the outpost was established, they would attack shepherds and landowners who tried to reach the area, and then they set up a small outpost that began to expand," he told the Israeli newspaper.

Abu Nimel said the local Palestinian community now had no access to its land.

"When someone tries to get close to his own land, his orchards, they come down and drive him away at gunpoint," he said, referring to the settlers.

Settlers push to cancel Oslo Accords

Israeli settlers have long called for the cancellation of the Oslo Accords. Outgoing Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich also vowed during the recent election campaign to scrap the agreements.

In February, Smotrich unveiled his "Settlement 2030" plan, saying it included "eliminating the idea of an Arab terror state, cancelling the cursed Oslo Accords, and getting onto a path of [Israeli] sovereignty [in the West Bank], while encouraging emigration" from the occupied Gaza Strip and the West Bank.

More than 737,000 Israeli settlers live in over 400 settlements and outposts, mostly in Area C of the occupied West Bank. Israeli settlements are illegal under international law.

According to Haaretz, settlers celebrated the establishment of the Homesh yeshiva branch as part of their efforts to overturn the Oslo Accords. 

‘My land is forbidden to me’: Israel’s settlement push encircles Jenin
Read More »

Elishama Cohen, head of the yeshiva, said in a video filmed at the outpost that the institution had taken it upon itself "to continue the redemption of the land and to continue to repair the sin" of the Oslo Accords.

"Unless we move forward and return, inherit and settle every part of our holy land, it will not be achievable," Cohen reportedly said.

Last week, an Israeli settler account on X posted a video of settlers dancing at the outpost, declaring: "Far away in the mountains, deep in Area A, the spark of the holy Torah breaks forth and rises, bringing us closer step by step to the redemption of the whole Land of Israel and the cancellation of the Oslo Accords."

Settlers have maintained a presence at the outpost since at least September last year, when Israeli media reported that an influential settler rabbi had celebrated the establishment of the Homesh yeshiva branch.

"The Oslo Accords were against the covenant that God made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and they are destined to be annulled," Shmuel Eliyahu, the chief rabbi of Safed, said during a reported visit to the outpost at the end of September.

The latest land grab in the northern West Bank forms part of a wider Israeli campaign to seize Palestinian land and establish settlements in the area, Middle East Eye reported in August.

Three years ago, the Israeli government repealed the Disengagement Law, under which Israel evacuated several settlements in the area in 2005. Since then, the Israeli government has re-established the settlements of Sa-Nur, Ganim, Kadim and Homesh.

articles.title: Israeli prison guard ‘slapped and tore off hijab’ of Palestinian detainee
articles.summary:
Israeli prison guard ‘slapped and tore off hijab’ of Palestinian detainee 

Submitted by Fayha Shalash on Wed, 11/18/2026 - 13:34
A former detainee says Israeli prisons routinely strip women of their hijabs, deny them prayer clothing and subject them to physical abuse and degrading conditions
A Palestinian woman wearing a hijab holds a placard bearing a slogan calling for the freedom of Palestinian prisoners held in Israeli jails (Nasser Ishtayeh/SOPA Images via Reuters)
Off

An Israeli prison director reportedly slapped a Palestinian woman detainee and forcibly removed her hijab during an assault at Damon Prison, according to Palestinian prisoners’ rights monitors.

The Prisoners’ Media Office said on Tuesday that the prison administration had ordered female detainees to remove their hijabs before being photographed, claiming the procedure was necessary to update their personal records.

Women who refused were physically assaulted.

According to the office, prison staff removed detainees from their cells one by one and took them to a photography room. Those who refused to remove their hijabs were beaten in an attempt to force them to comply.

In one incident, the prison director forcibly removed a detainee’s hijab, slapped her and pushed her into the photography room.

The assault reportedly took place shortly after the woman had completed eight days in solitary confinement.

Amani Sarahneh, a spokesperson for the Palestinian Prisoners’ Club, said lawyers who visited detainees at Damon Prison confirmed that women had been coerced into removing their hijabs during photography procedures.

She added that this was not the first time female detainees had faced such practices.

'Violations are no longer limited to the hijab; they encompass all aspects of life inside the prison'

- Amani Sarahneh, Palestinian Prisoners’ Club

Sarahneh said targeting the hijab violated the women’s privacy and dignity, reflecting the prison administration’s use of various methods to mistreat and humiliate them.

"Violations are no longer limited to the hijab; they encompass all aspects of life inside the prison, in the absence of the 'red lines' that once constrained the conduct of the prison administration," she told Middle East Eye.

She said the incident was particularly serious because the abuse extended beyond forcing detainees to remove their hijabs to filming the coercive measures.

Raids and acts of repression are now routinely recorded, including instances in which detainees are taken into the prison yard and filmed, she said.

Sarahneh argued that such filming had become an integral part of the abuse, rather than merely an administrative procedure.

Assaults on women prisoners  

A former Palestinian female detainee, who requested anonymity, told MEE that violations of women’s right to wear the hijab occur daily inside Israeli prisons.

She explained that one of the first procedures detainees face after arrest is being forced to remove all their clothing, including their hijabs, before being issued the brown prison uniform imposed by the administration.

As a result, detainees are often forced to use pieces of their prison uniforms as head coverings, attempting to maintain their hijab despite the lack of suitable garments.

"The prison administration also denies female detainees access to prayer clothes, forcing them to use whatever fabric is available, even an old, torn bedsheet found in their cell, to cover their bodies during prayer," she said.

'All changed with the genocide': Palestinian women and girls face brutal abuse in Israeli jails
Read More »

She added that detainees lack the basic necessities to practise their religious observances while preserving their privacy and dignity. 

Surveillance cameras installed throughout the prison further compound the violations of their privacy, she said.

"These measures, taken together, deprive them of their most fundamental religious rights, leaving them no opportunity to practise their faith freely or in privacy," she said.

The former detainee said physical assaults had become a daily occurrence, often carried out under various pretexts and for the most trivial reasons. Women are frequently dragged, have their hair pulled and endure repeated physical abuse, she added.

She also described the food provided to female detainees as extremely poor, with meals often undercooked and served without salt or seasoning. Most meals, she said, consist of lentils.

Their suffering is compounded by the presence of sick detainees who urgently need medical treatment and care but receive no adequate medical follow-up, leaving them to endure illness and pain without proper intervention.

At least 90 Palestinian women, including three minors, are currently held in Israeli prisons, according to the Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs.

Earlier this month, the Commission reported that 24 per cent of female detainees were held under administrative detention, which allows Israel to detain Palestinians without charge or trial for indefinite periods.

articles.title: Israel launches assault targeting residential areas in Gaza despite ceasefire
articles.summary:
Israel launches assault targeting residential areas in Gaza despite ceasefire

The Israeli military launched a new ground assault on residential areas in the central Gaza Strip on Wednesday, forcing displaced Palestinian families to flee despite the ceasefire agreement.

Tanks were seen advancing into areas near the Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps, according to local media.

At least two people were wounded by indiscriminate fire near Nuseirat refugee camp, while scores of residents fled the area following the surprise assault.

The Israeli military confirmed the attack, which is taking place beyond the so-called "Yellow Line" – a military boundary imposed by Israeli forces inside the Gaza Strip following the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.

The army claimed it was targeting "terrorist infrastructure" in areas it designated as “Blocks 660, 661 and 666”. These are residential areas where Palestinian residents and displaced families live.

Read more: Israel launches assault targeting residential areas in Gaza despite ceasefire

articles.title: Labour MPs quit Somaliland group over Israel and chair’s ties to far-right Restore
articles.summary:
Labour MPs quit Somaliland group over Israel and chair’s ties to far-right Restore

Kim Johnson, an MP from the UK’s Labour Party, was helping to host an event in the UK parliament marking the anniversary of Somaliland’s self-declared independence when she was told that an official from another government was on their way to attend.

“When I heard there would be an Israeli government official there, I just left the event as quickly as I could,” Johnson told Middle East Eye.

The unexpected appearance of an Israeli official at the May event was the final straw for Johnson, a backbencher on Labour’s left and an advocate for Palestinian rights, who quit the UK’s all-party parliamentary group (APPG) on Somaliland soon after.

Abtisam Mohamed, the Labour MP for Sheffield Central and Johnson’s deputy in the group, also resigned her post this week, Middle East Eye can reveal, while Kerry McCarthy, Labour MP for Bristol East, has stopped participating in the group’s activities until its chair, the Conservative MP Gavin Williamson, resigns.

MEE understands that the APPG, Westminster’s main forum advocating for Somaliland and its diaspora, has not met since before the UK parliament’s summer recess amid fallout over Israel's recognition of Somaliland and Williamson's ties to the hardline anti-immigration party Restore Britain.

Read more: Exclusive: Labour MPs quit Somaliland group over Israel and chair’s ties to far-right Restore
